heroData.title: EOR & PEO in Guinea
heroData.subtitle: Comprehensive guide to EOR & PEO in Guinea
heroData.description: Detailed insights and providers for EOR & PEO in Guinea.

sections.title: Onboarding Process via EOR in Guinea
sections.subtitle: Average timeline: 10-15 business days

steps.title: Contract Drafting & Compliance Review
steps.description: Drafting of a locally compliant employment contract in French. The contract must specify the SMIG (minimum wage), working hours (40 hours per week), and mandatory benefits. EOR ensures alignment with the Guinea Labour Code 2014.

steps.title: Documentation & Identity Verification
steps.description: Collection of employee documents: National ID or Passport, proof of residence, social security number (if existing), and academic credentials. For foreign nationals, the EOR initiates the work permit sponsorship process.

steps.title: CNSS & Tax Registration
steps.description: Registration of the employee with the Caisse Nationale de Sécurité Sociale (CNSS). Setting up the withholding of Revenue sur le Traitement et Salaire (RTS) for monthly income tax filing.

steps.title: Health & Safety Briefing
steps.description: Providing mandatory information on workplace safety and medical coverage. The EOR ensures the employee is aware of the local medical services and health insurance providers partnered for supplemental cover.

steps.title: Payroll Integration & Final Sign-off
steps.description: Employee is added to the Guinea-based payroll system. First pay run is scheduled, and all digital access for payroll slips is provided. Final employment contract is signed by both parties.

items.title: Permanent Establishment (PE) Risk
items.text: Hiring multiple employees in Guinea via EOR without a local subsidiary can eventually trigger PE risk if the employees are involved in core sales or revenue-generating activities for the parent company. Periodic legal audits are recommended.

items.title: Fixed-Term Contract (CDD) Limits
items.text: CDDs in Guinea are strictly regulated. They can only be renewed twice for a maximum total duration of 24 months. Exceeding this automatically converts the role into a permanent contract (CDI).

items.title: Social Security Filing Accuracy
items.text: CNSS reporting must be precise. Discrepancies between withheld amounts and reported earnings can lead to heavy penalties (up to 10% of the unpaid balance) and delays in employee benefit claims.

items.title: French Language Requirement
items.text: French is the official language for all legal and employment documents. While business may be conducted in English or local languages like Fulani or Susu, the Labour Court only recognizes French contracts.

items.title: Thirteenth Month Salary
items.text: While not a statutory requirement in Guinea, providing a 13th-month bonus at the end of the year (usually in December) is a common market practice to attract and retain top-tier talent.

items.title: Islamic Holiday Sensitivity
items.text: Guinea has a significant Muslim population. Respecting prayer times and recognizing Islamic holidays (determined by the lunar calendar) is crucial for employee relations and cultural alignment.

faqs.question: Can I hire foreign nationals through an EOR in Guinea?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the EOR must sponsor their work permit (Permis de Travail). This process requires proof that the skills were not readily available in the local market and involves a fee to the Ministry of Labor.

faqs.question: How are notice periods handled for termination?
faqs.answer: Notice periods depend on the job grade: 3 months for executives/managers, 2 months for supervisors/technicians, and 1 month for secondary-level employees. Payments in lieu of notice are permitted.

faqs.question: Is remote work supported by local laws?
faqs.answer: The 2014 Labour Code is predominantly based on physical presence, but remote work is permissible under private agreement within the EOR framework. Employers must ensure digital compliance and equipment provision.

sections.title: Monthly Payroll Processing Workflow
sections.subtitle: Standard cycle: 20th to 30th of each month

steps.title: Data Gathering & Variable Input
steps.description: Collection of monthly variables including overtime hours (hours 41-48 at 130%, hours 49+ at 160%), bonuses, commissions, and any unpaid leave deductions. All inputs must be finalized by the 20th of the month.

steps.title: Gross-to-Net Calculation
steps.description: Processing of gross salaries through the Guinean tax engine. This includes calculating the RTS (Income Tax) based on progressive brackets and deducting the mandatory 5% employee CNSS contribution.

steps.title: Compliance Formatting & Review
steps.description: Generation of payslips in French (locally required format). Review of employer-side liabilities including the 6% VAFC (Flat-rate contribution) and the standard 18% CNSS employer share.

steps.title: Treasury & Disbursement
steps.description: Executing bank transfers in GNF (Guinean Franc). For international employees, currency conversion and cross-border transfer approvals from the Central Bank of Guinea may be required for large sums.

steps.title: Statutory Filing & Payment
steps.description: Finalizing the monthly 'Déclaration Récapitulative' for tax and social security. Payments must be remitted to the CNSS and the Tax Office (Direction Nationale des Impôts) by the 15th of the following month.

rows.label: Union Dues
values: Only if specified in Collective Agreement

items.title: CNSS Monthly Deadline
items.text: All social security contributions must be paid by the 15th of the month following the payroll period. Late payments incur a penalty of 10% plus interest on the principal amount.

items.title: Annual Summary Filing
items.text: Employers must file a 'Déclaration Annuelle des Salaires' (DADS) before January 31st of the following year, summarizing all salaries paid and taxes withheld for the prior 12 months.

items.title: Overtime Record Maintenance
items.text: The Labour Inspectorate often audits overtime logs. Ensure that hours worked beyond 40 per week are documented with employee signatures and justified by business necessity.

faqs.question: Are electronic payslips legal in Guinea?
faqs.answer: Yes, electronic payslips are increasingly common and legal, provided they contain all mandatory fields: gross pay, breakdown of deductions (CNSS, RTS), and employer identification details.

faqs.question: What happens if an employee's salary is below the SMIG?
faqs.answer: It is illegal to pay below the SMIG (Salaire Minimum Interprofessionnel Garanti). Employers doing so face heavy fines and must retroactively adjust all payments to the minimum threshold.

faqs.question: Can I pay employees in USD/EUR?
faqs.answer: Remuneration must be stated in GNF in the contract. Actual payment can be made in foreign currency for expatriates, but the equivalent GNF value must be used for tax and social security calculations.

sections.title: Net Salary Calculation Roadmap
sections.subtitle: From gross remuneration to final take-home pay

steps.title: Gross Salary & Allowances Definition
steps.description: Defining the base salary plus mandatory and optional allowances (housing, transport, and seniority). Note: Allowances are often tax-exempt up to 25% of the total compensation.

steps.title: Employee CNSS Deduction (5%)
steps.description: Applying the mandatory 5% employee contribution to the National Social Security Fund (CNSS). This covers health insurance, disability, and basic pension.

steps.title: Taxable Base & RTS Calculation
steps.description: Determining the taxable base after CNSS and exempt allowances. Applying the progressive RTS (Revenu de Traitement et Salaire) brackets ranging from 0% to 20%.

steps.title: Professional Expenses Deduction
steps.description: Applying the standard 10% deduction for professional expenses (capped by law) if applicable, further reducing the final taxable amount.

steps.title: Net-to-Bank Disbursement
steps.description: Final calculation of the 'Net à Payer'. Issuing a bilingual (French/English) payslip as required by the Guinean Labour Code for compliance.

items.title: The 25% Exemption Rule
items.text: Under Guinean tax law, allowances (housing, transport, water/electricity) can be structured to be non-taxable as long as they do not exceed 25% of the total monthly gross salary.

items.title: New 2025 Tax Bracket
items.text: Recent reforms introduced an middle bracket of 8% for earnings between 3,000,000 GNF and 5,000,000 GNF, which may increase deductions for mid-level local staff.

items.title: Expatriate Tax Regimes
items.text: Foreign employees staying less than 183 days may qualify for a simplified non-resident withholding tax (15%), but must still be registered with CNSS for local coverage.

items.title: Overtime Multipliers
items.text: Overtime is calculated on the 40-hour base week. Hours 41-48 are paid at 130%, while hours above 48 are paid at 160%. Night shifts (10 PM - 6 AM) attract a 50% premium.

items.title: The 13th Month
items.text: While not strictly mandatory by the Labour Code, the 'Prime de Fin d'Année' (13th month) is a standard expectation and is usually distributed in December.

items.title: Severance Pay Formula
items.text: Severance is calculated based on seniority: 25% of monthly salary per year for the first 5 years, increasing gradually for longer tenures.

faqs.question: What is the standard frequency for payroll in Guinea?
faqs.answer: Payroll is typically processed monthly. Payments are generally made between the 25th and the last day of the month via bank transfer in Guinean Francs (GNF).

faqs.question: Can salaries be paid in foreign currency (USD/EUR)?
faqs.answer: While the contract can state a USD value, the actual payment within Guinea must generally be made in GNF at the central bank's exchange rate, unless a special exemption is granted.

faqs.question: Are meal vouchers common in Conakry?
faqs.answer: Yes, 'Prime de Panier' (Meal allowance) is common and is typically a fixed daily or monthly amount that is exempted from tax up to a specific threshold.

heroData.title: Incorporation in Guinea
heroData.subtitle: Comprehensive guide to Incorporation in Guinea
heroData.description: Detailed insights and providers for Incorporation in Guinea.

steps.title: Corporate Name Reservation
steps.description: Verify and reserve a unique company name with the Agence de Promotion des Investissements Privés (APIP). A certificate of uniqueness is issued upon approval.

steps.title: Statutes Drafting & Notarization
steps.description: Drafting the Articles of Association (Statuts) in accordance with the OHADA Uniform Act. While private agreements are possible for SARLs, notarization by a licensed Guinean notary is highly recommended for legal weight.

steps.title: Capital Deposit
steps.description: Opening a temporary 'Equity in Formulation' bank account in a local commercial bank. Depositing the minimum share capital and obtaining a deposit certificate (Attestation de versement des fonds).

steps.title: One-Stop Shop Submission
steps.description: Filing the complete dossier at APIP. This single submission handles the RCCM (Commercial Registry), NIF (Tax ID), and CNSS (Social Security) registrations simultaneously.

steps.title: Legal Publication
steps.description: Publishing a notice of incorporation in the Journal d’Annonces Légales or a widely circulated local newspaper to inform the public and complete the legal formality.

items.title: OHADA Framework
items.text: Guinea is a member of OHADA (Organization for the Harmonization of Business Law in Africa). All corporate structures, insolvency rules, and accounting standards follow the OHADA Uniform Acts, ensuring legal consistency with 16 other African nations.

items.title: Simplified SARL (SARLU)
items.text: For solo founders, the SARL Unipersonnelle is an excellent option. It offers limited liability protection with only one shareholder and is the most common vehicle for small-to-medium foreign investment entries.

items.title: Local Director Presence
items.text: While there is no strict residency requirement for directors in the law, having a local 'Gérant' or a resident legal representative is practically essential for daily administrative tasks and local banking relationships.

items.title: Business License (Patente)
items.text: Within 3 months of setup, companies must apply for more specific sectoral licenses if they operate in mining, telecoms, or banking. The annual 'Patente' fee is also due based on the company's rental value and turnover.

items.title: Annual General Meeting (AGM)
items.text: OHADA law requires all companies to hold an AGM within six months of the financial year-end (usually by June 30) to approve accounts and decide on profit allocation.

items.title: Bank Account Activation
items.text: Activating the permanent corporate bank account can take longer than the incorporation itself (2-4 weeks). Banks in Conakry have strict KYC requirements for foreign UBOs.

faqs.question: Can a foreigner own 100% of a Guinean company?
faqs.answer: Yes, Guinea allows 100% foreign ownership in most sectors. However, certain strategic sectors like mining and telecommunications may have specific requirements for local partnership or government participation.

faqs.question: What is the typical timeline for incorporation?
faqs.answer: The APIP 'One-Stop Shop' process takes about 2 to 5 business days for the certificate issuance, but preparing the dossier and notarizing statutes usually extends the total timeline to 2 weeks.

faqs.question: Do I need a physical office address?
faqs.answer: Yes, a registered office address in Guinea is mandatory. A commercial lease agreement or a domiciliation contract with a local service provider must be submitted during registration.

heroData.title: Staffing in Guinea
heroData.subtitle: Comprehensive guide to Staffing in Guinea
heroData.description: Detailed insights and providers for Staffing in Guinea.

steps.title: Sourcing Strategy & Multi-Channel Posting
steps.description: Leveraging local platforms like 'Emploi-Guinee', LinkedIn (primary for white-collar), and sector-specific networks in mining and infrastructure. Job ads must be in French to attract the core local talent pool.

steps.title: Candidate Screen & Language Assessment
steps.description: Initial screening focusing on technical certifications (especially for ECOWAS/OHADA standards) and French/English proficiency. For expatriate roles, cultural adaptability is also assessed.

steps.title: Background & Credential Verification
steps.description: Verification of academic diplomas from institutions like the University of Conakry. Criminal record checks (Casier Judiciaire) are standard for finance, security, and executive positions.

steps.title: Technical Interviewing & Testing
steps.description: Coordination of interviews with local subject matter experts. For industrial roles, medical fitness tests are often mandated by safety regulations before a final offer is extended.

steps.title: Offer Negotiation & Local Compliance Check
steps.description: Providing a formal offer letter including gross salary in GNF, statutory benefits (CNSS), and any supplemental allowances (housing, transport) which are highly expected in the Guinean market.

rows.label: Retained Search Fee
values: For C-level or specialized mining roles

rows.label: Contractor Management
values: On top of worker's monthly rate

rows.label: Job Advertisement Package
values: Monthly posting on premium local boards

items.title: Mining Sector Dominance
items.text: The Simandou Iron Ore project and Bauxite exports drive the majority of high-skilled hiring. Candidates with previous experience in BHP, Rio Tinto, or SMB Winning are highly sought after and command significant salary premiums.

items.title: Education vs. Practical Skills Gap
items.text: While Guinea produces many university graduates, there is a noted shortage of middle-management and technical vocational skills. Investing in internal training programs or 'graduate trainee' schemes is often necessary for long-term growth.

items.title: Mobile-First Sourcing
items.text: Over 90% of job seekers in Guinea use mobile devices. Ensure all recruitment portals and communications are mobile-responsive and leverage WhatsApp for initial coordination, which is the preferred local communication tool.

items.title: Allowances Importance
items.text: In Conakry, 'Transport' and 'Housing' allowances are often expected as separate line items in the salary package rather than being rolled into the base salary. This has tax implications and improves offer acceptance rates.

items.title: Reference Verification Culture
items.text: Direct phone calls to previous employers are more effective than written reference letters in Guinea. The professional community is tight-knit, and verbal confirmations are generally more reliable.

items.title: Union Representation
items.text: Be aware of union presence in the mining and industrial sectors. Early engagement with union representatives during large-scale hiring can preempt future industrial relations issues.

faqs.question: What is the standard notice period for candidates?
faqs.answer: The standard is 1 month for junior/mid roles and 3 months for executives. Candidates often expect the new employer to 'buy out' their notice period if an immediate start is required.

faqs.question: Are there quotas for hiring local Guineans?
faqs.answer: Yes, Guinea has 'Guineanization' policies, particularly in mining. For every expatriate hired, companies must often demonstrate a plan to train and eventually replace them with a local national over 3-5 years.

faqs.question: What are the common work hours in Guinea?
faqs.answer: The statutory work week is 40 hours. Anything beyond is considered overtime. Saturday work is common in the service and retail sectors but requires overtime pay if it exceeds 40 hours total.

heroData.title: HRIS in Guinea
heroData.subtitle: Comprehensive guide to HRIS in Guinea
heroData.description: Detailed insights and providers for HRIS in Guinea.

steps.title: Data Audit & Cleanup
steps.description: Consolidating paper-based records into a digital format. Ensuring all employee data (NIF, CNSS numbers, leave balances) is accurate and formatted for migration.

steps.title: Localization & Legal Configuration
steps.description: Configuring the system for the Guinea Labour Code 2014, including RTS (Social Contribution) logic, 13th-month bonus automation, and CNSS social security rates.

steps.title: User Acceptance Testing (UAT)
steps.description: Testing the system with a pilot group of HR managers and employees. Verification of automated payslip generation and employee self-service (ESS) modules under local internet conditions.

steps.title: Privacy Compliance Verification
steps.description: Reviewing data storage and access protocols to ensure alignment with Law No. L/2016/037/AN regarding personal data protection and cross-border data flows.

steps.title: Full Rollout & Support Training
steps.description: Launching the system company-wide. Providing training sessions for staff in French and establishing a helpdesk to handle initial login and usage queries.

items.title: Mobile-First Accessibility
items.text: With limited fixed-line internet, HRIS platforms must offer robust mobile applications. Employees in mining and remote sectors rely heavily on smartphones for payslip access and leave requests.

items.title: Data Privacy Enforcement
items.text: While the APDP is still building its administrative capacity, companies are increasingly under scrutiny for how they handle employee PII (Personally Identifiable Information). Cloud-based HRIS providers must have SOC2/ISO 27001 certifications or local equivalents.

items.title: Biometric Integration
items.text: For industrial sites in Conakry and Kindia, integrating HRIS with biometric time-clocks is a common practice to prevent 'buddy-punching' and ensure accurate overtime calculations.

items.title: Language Support
items.text: The interface must be available in French. While many managers speak English in the mining sector, the general workforce requires French-language menus and help documentation.

items.title: Offline-first Requirements
items.text: In regions with frequent power and internet outages, look for HRIS solutions that cache data locally and sync once connectivity is restored to prevent data loss.

items.title: Currency Formatting
items.text: The system must support GNF (Guinean Franc) without precision errors, as the denominations are large. Ensuring the system handles large integers for salary fields is crucial.

faqs.question: Are digital payslips legally valid in Guinea?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided the employee has given consent and the digital system ensures the integrity of the document. Most modern HRIS generate PDFs that meet these criteria.

faqs.question: Where should employee data be hosted?
faqs.answer: There is no absolute requirement for local hosting in Guinea, but cross-border data transfers to countries without equivalent data protection laws theoretically require APDP notification.

faqs.question: Does HRIS help with CNSS filings?
faqs.answer: Yes, a localized HRIS can generate the monthly CNSS remittance files (DADS/DMS) automatically, significantly reducing the manual effort of compliance reporting.

heroData.title: Accounting in Guinea
heroData.subtitle: Comprehensive guide to Accounting in Guinea
heroData.description: Detailed insights and providers for Accounting in Guinea.

steps.title: Monthly Bookkeeping & Reconciliation
steps.description: Ongoing recording of transactions using the SYSCOHADA chart of accounts. Monthly bank reconciliations and VAT (TVA) return preparation (due by the 15th of the following month).

steps.title: Year-End Closing & Trial Balance
steps.description: Finalizing all adjusting entries, including depreciation, accruals, and provisions. Generation of the final trial balance as of December 31.

steps.title: Financial Statement Preparation (DSF)
steps.description: Drafting the 'Déclaration Statistique et Fiscale' (DSF) which includes the Balance Sheet, Income Statement, Cash Flow Statement, and Notes. For companies in Guinea, the DSF must be prepared in French.

steps.title: Statutory Audit (If Applicable)
steps.description: Engagement of a 'Commissaire aux Comptes' for mandatory audit. This is required for all SAs and for SARLs/SASs meeting specific OHADA turnover or asset thresholds.

steps.title: Annual Filing & AGM
steps.description: Submission of the audited DSF to the National Tax Directorate (DNI) by April 30. Holding the Annual General Meeting (AGM) to approve accounts before June 30.

items.title: SYSCOHADA Standards
items.text: Guinea follows the revised SYSCOHADA (2017), which is the accounting framework for OHADA member states. It is a dual-purpose system aimed at both financial reporting and tax base determination.

items.title: Audit Thresholds
items.text: SARLs must appoint a statutory auditor if they meet two of the following: Assets > GNF 1.8B, Turnover > GNF 3.6B, or > 50 employees. Failure to appoint an auditor when required can lead to the nullification of AGM decisions.

items.title: ONEC Certification
items.text: Always ensure your accountant or auditor is a member of the 'Ordre National des Experts-Comptables de Guinée' (ONEC). Only ONEC members are legally authorized to sign off on statutory financial statements.

items.title: 10-Year Retention
items.text: Under OHADA law, all accounting records, vouchers, and financial statements must be kept for a minimum of 10 years. Both physical and digital archives are acceptable.

items.title: French Language Requirement
items.text: All statutory books (Journal Book, Ledger, Inventory Book) must be maintained in French. While internal reporting can be in English, the official DSF submission must be in French.

items.title: Digital Filing Progress
items.text: The Guinean tax administration (DNI) is progressively moving towards e-filing for large taxpayers (DGE). E-filing requires a specific digital certificate linked to the company's NIF.

faqs.question: Can I use IFRS for my Guinean subsidiary?
faqs.answer: Listed companies must use IFRS. For unlisted companies, SYSCOHADA is mandatory for local statutory filing, but you can maintain a second set of books for IFRS/US GAAP reporting to the parent company.

faqs.question: What is the penalty for late DSF filing?
faqs.answer: Late filing of the annual financial statement (DSF) results in fixed fines and potential interest on any unpaid corporate tax. More importantly, it can trigger a full tax audit.

faqs.question: Are cloud accounting tools like Xero or QuickBooks used locally?
faqs.answer: Yes, they are used for internal management. However, for statutory reporting, specialized SYSCOHADA-compliant software (like Sage or local African ERPs) is often preferred to ensure easy generation of the DSF.

sections.title: Regulatory Compliance Roadmap
sections.subtitle: Essential ongoing checks for foreign entities

steps.title: UBO Register Maintenance
steps.description: Maintaining an updated register of Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBO) at the RCCM. Required under Law L/2021/001/AN to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing.

steps.title: Local Content Plan Submission
steps.description: Drafting and submitting a 'Plan de Contenu Local' to the Ministry of Mines or Infrastructure. This plan must detail how the company will prioritize Guinean staff and suppliers.

steps.title: Foreign Contract Validation (AGUIPE)
steps.description: Submitting all expatriate employment contracts to AGUIPE for a mandatory 'visa'. This ensures the role cannot be reasonably filled by a Guinean national.

steps.title: Data Processing Declaration (APDP)
steps.description: Registering with the Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP). Companies must declare what employee and client data they collect and how it is stored securely.

steps.title: Annual Compliance Audit & Reporting
steps.description: Conducting an internal audit to verify adherence to tax filings, labor code mandates, and environmental permits. Reporting significant deviations to relevant local authorities.

items.title: Local Content Enforcement (2025)
items.text: The 2022 Local Content Law is now fully enforced. Foreign companies are increasingly required to form JVs with Guinean-owned firms for certain government contracts and sub-contracts in the mining sector.

items.title: Anti-Corruption Scrutiny
items.text: Guinea has strengthened its 'CRIEF' (Special Court for Economic Crimes). International businesses must have robust internal anti-bribery policies that align with both local law and the FCPA/UK Bribery Act.

items.title: Environment & ESG reporting
items.text: For the Simandou and Kindia mining corridors, ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) compliance is a prerequisite for funding and operating permits. Annual EIR (Environmental Impact Reports) are mandatory.

items.title: KYC for Local Partners
items.text: Conduct deep due diligence when selecting local Guinean partners. Verify their beneficial ownership to ensure they are not Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), which could pose significant global compliance risks.

items.title: Health & Safety Surveys
items.text: Occupational health and safety (OHS) inspections by the Labor Inspectorate are common. Companies must maintain a 'Safety Register' on-site and provide mandatory PPE to all industrial staff.

items.title: Work Permit Renewals
items.text: Expatriate work permits are usually valid for one year. The renewal process must start at least 45 days before expiry to avoid fines and potential deportation risks for senior management.

faqs.question: What is the penalty for using unregistered expatriates?
faqs.answer: Using expatriates without valid AGUIPE-stamped contracts can lead to heavy fines for the company and the immediate suspension of the individuals' work rights. In severe cases, the company's business license may be reviewed.

faqs.question: Does Guinea have a publicly accessible UBO register?
faqs.answer: The register exists at the RCCM but is not fully open to the public; it is primarily accessible to regulatory authorities, banks, and legal professionals for verification purposes.

faqs.question: Is ISO certification recognized locally?
faqs.answer: Yes, ISO 9001, 14001, and 45001 certifications are highly regarded and often required for Tier 1 suppliers in the mining and infrastructure industries in Guinea.

steps.title: NIF Registration (Tax ID)
steps.description: Obtaining the 'Numéro d'Identification Fiscale' (NIF) from the National Tax Directorate (DNI) via APIP. The NIF is mandatory for all corporate activities and customs clearances.

steps.title: Monthly Declarations (VAT & RTS)
steps.description: Submission of monthly returns for Value Added Tax (TVA) at 18% and Personal Income Tax (RTS) withheld from employees. Returns must be filed and paid by the 15th of each month.

steps.title: Quarterly Installment Payments
steps.description: Payment of corporate tax (IS) installments. These are typically due on June 15 and September 15, calculated as a percentage of the previous year's tax liability or turnover.

steps.title: Annual DSF Preparation & Filing
steps.description: Finalizing the 'Déclaration Statistique et Fiscale' (DSF) for the fiscal year ending December 31. The filing deadline is April 30 of the following year.

steps.title: Final Tax Balancing & Audit Ready
steps.description: Settling any remaining Corporate Income Tax (IS) balance and ensuring all tax receipts are archived for potential DNI audits, which are frequent for foreign-owned entities.

rows.label: Value Added Tax (VAT)
values: Standard rate on goods and services

rows.label: Minimum Tax (IMF)
values: Payable if no profit is made (capped)

items.title: Investment Code Benefits
items.text: Under the 2015 Investment Code, companies in Conakry (Zone A) can benefit from a 3-year exemption from corporate tax and business license fees. Companies in remote regions (Zone B/C) enjoy up to 8 years of exemptions.

items.title: Minimum Flat Tax (IMF)
items.text: Even loss-making companies must pay the IMF, which is 3% of turnover. There is a floor of GNF 3,000,000 and a ceiling of GNF 40,000,000, ensuring the state receives at least a base contribution from registered entities.

items.title: Local Content Surcharges
items.text: Non-compliance with local content laws (hiring and procurement targets) can lead to penalties that effectively act as an additional tax burden. Proactive local hiring planning is essential for tax efficiency.

items.title: Double Tax Treaties (DTT)
items.text: Guinea has a limited network of tax treaties (e.g., France, Morocco). Investors from these jurisdictions can often reduce withholding tax on dividends and interest from 10% to 5% with proper documentation.

items.title: Transfer Pricing Rules
items.text: Following OHADA and OECD guidelines, Guinea requires transactions between related parties to be at 'arm's length'. Documentation must be available to justify pricing for management fees or intercompany loans.

items.title: VAT Refund Challenges
items.text: While VAT refunds are legally possible, the process is often slow and requires a thorough audit of input VAT. Many companies choose to offset credit against future VAT liabilities instead of requesting cash refunds.

faqs.question: What is the VAT registration threshold?
faqs.answer: The annual turnover threshold for mandatory VAT registration is GNF 1,000,000,000. Companies below this can opt-in if they want to claim input VAT.

faqs.question: Can I pay taxes in foreign currency?
faqs.answer: No, all taxes must be declared and paid in Guinean Francs (GNF). For companies with ledger currency in USD/EUR, the exchange rate at the time of the taxable event is used.

faqs.question: Are there specific taxes for mining companies?
faqs.answer: Yes, mining entities are subject to specific royalties (redevance minière) and surface taxes, often negotiated in the specific Mining Convention signed with the state.

heroData.title: MSA & Legal in Guinea
heroData.subtitle: Comprehensive guide to MSA & Legal in Guinea
heroData.description: Detailed insights and providers for MSA & Legal in Guinea.

steps.title: OHADA Compliance Review
steps.description: Analyzing the MSA draft against the OHADA Uniform Act on General Commercial Law. Ensuring all mandatory provisions for service contracts in West Africa are included.

steps.title: Bilingual Versioning (French/English)
steps.description: Preparing a sworn French translation of the MSA. In Guinea, the French version is legally binding and required for submission in any local court or administrative process.

steps.title: Local Notarization & Legalization
steps.description: Signing the document before a local notary (Notaire) if it involves real estate or security interests. For standard MSAs, legalization at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs may be required for cross-border use.

steps.title: Arbitration Clause Configuration
steps.description: Inserting a robust dispute resolution clause. It is highly recommended to specify arbitration under the CCJA (Abidjan) to bypass lengthy local judicial backlogs.

steps.title: Digital/Physical Archiving
steps.description: Registering the contract with the tax authorities (Enregistrement) to give it a 'fixed date' (date certaine), which is crucial for proving the contract's existence against third parties.

items.title: OHADA Commercial Harmonization
items.text: Being part of OHADA means commercial laws are largely identical to 16 other African nations. This provides a predictable legal environment for regional service agreements.

items.title: Judicial Delays
items.text: Local litigation in Guinea can take 3-5 years to reach a verdict. MSA contracts should always include summary judgment or mandatory mediation phases to mitigate this risk.

items.title: Liability Caps in Service Contracts
items.text: Under Guinean law, gross negligence cannot be capped. However, standard professional liability can be limited to the value of the services rendered, provided the clause is clearly negotiated.

items.title: OAPI Intellectual Property
items.text: Intellectual property is managed by OAPI. A single registration in any member state (like Guinea or Cameroon) protects your trademark/patent across all 17 member countries.

items.title: Termination Formalities
items.text: Termination for breach requires a formal 'Mise en Demeure' (formal notice) delivered via a bailiff (Huissier de Justice) to be legally enforceable in Guinea.

items.title: Electronic Signatures
items.text: Electronic signatures are increasingly recognized under modern Guinean law, but for high-value contracts, a physical 'wet signature' with a company stamp (cachet) is still the market standard.

faqs.question: Can we use a foreign law (e.g., English Law) for our MSA?
faqs.answer: Yes, OHADA law allows for freedom of choice of law in international contracts. However, if the services are performed in Guinea, local mandatory rules (labor/tax) will always override the foreign law.

faqs.question: Is a company stamp mandatory?
faqs.answer: While not strictly a legal requirement for all contracts, in practice, no Guinean bank or authority will accept a document without a 'Cachet de l'Entreprise'.

faqs.question: What is the role of a 'Huissier de Justice'?
faqs.answer: A bailiff is essential for serving legal notices, proving the delivery of documents, and collecting debts through formal seizures (Saisie-Attribution).

steps.title: Infrastructure Audit & Power Readiness
steps.description: Assessing local server rooms or cloud latency. Due to frequent power outages in Conakry, ensuring redundant UPS systems and generators are in place for any on-premise components.

steps.title: Data Privacy Impact Assessment (DPIA)
steps.description: Reviewing data flows against Law L/2016/037/AN. Notifying the Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP) if any sensitive Guinean citizen data is stored on offshore servers.

steps.title: ERP/Software Localization
steps.description: Configuring software for the Guinean context, including French language interfaces, SYSCOHADA accounting charts, and local VAT (18%) logic for invoice generation.

steps.title: User Training in French
steps.description: Conducting comprehensive training sessions for local staff. Providing documentation and helpdesk support in French is critical for high adoption rates in the Guinean market.

steps.title: UAT & Connectivity Stress Testing
steps.description: Performing User Acceptance Testing under real-world bandwidth conditions. Optimizing cloud-based apps for high latency or intermittent internet common in West Africa.

items.title: Open Source Preference
items.text: Open-source solutions like Odoo and ERPNext are gaining significant traction in Conakry due to lower initial licensing costs and the ability to find local developers for customization.

items.title: Data Sovereignty Trends
items.text: While there isn't a strict 'data residency' law for all sectors yet, banking and mining sectors are increasingly encouraged by regulators to host critical operational data on local Tier 3 servers.

items.title: Mobile-First Workforce
items.text: Guinean employees are highly mobile-centric. HR and project management tools must have high-quality mobile apps or PWA versions to ensure consistent usage outside the office.

items.title: Offline-First Design
items.text: When choosing software for field operations (especially in mining areas), prioritize tools that offer robust offline synchronization to handle frequent internet drops.

items.title: SLA Requirements
items.text: Demand high SLAs from local MSPs (Managed Service Providers). A typical acceptable uptime in Conakry's business districts is 98%, which often requires dual-WAN setups.

items.title: Anti-Piracy Compliance
items.text: The Guinean government is cracking down on unlicensed software in the corporate sector. Ensure all licenses are verified to avoid heavy fines from the Ministry of Information.

faqs.question: Are international SaaS providers like Salesforce or SAP available?
faqs.answer: Yes, they are available, but they are typically implemented through regional partners based in Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal, or France, as local Conakry-based certified partners are limited.

faqs.question: Does Guinea tax software-as-a-service (SaaS)?
faqs.answer: Yes, SaaS is subject to 18% VAT. If the provider is non-resident, the local Guinean customer is responsible for declaring and paying this VAT under the reverse-charge mechanism.

faqs.question: What is the primary language for software support?
faqs.answer: French is the primary language. While IT staff may speak English, end-user support and training should be provided in French to be effective.

steps.title: Consumer Insight & Language Audit
steps.description: Analyzing target demographics in Conakry and beyond. Ensuring all messaging is in Guinean French, with local cultural nuances and slang (e.g., 'Susu' or 'Pular' influences) to build authentic trust.

steps.title: Multi-Channel Media Mix Selection
steps.description: Defining the balance between traditional (Radio/Radio Rural for reach) and digital (Facebook/WhatsApp for engagement). B2B brands prioritize Conakry-based billboard corridors.

steps.title: Creative Production & Localization
steps.description: Producing high-quality visual content using local Guinean talent and landmarks. This resonates more than stock imagery and avoids 'expatriate-centric' brand perception.

steps.title: Influencer & Partnership Activation
steps.description: Vetting and contracting local Guinean influencers on TikTok and Facebook. Leveraging their community trust to drive brand awareness and direct product trials.

steps.title: Omnichannel Rollout & Performance Tracking
steps.description: Launching the campaign across all selected platforms. Monitoring KPIs like brand sentiment, lead generation, and store/office footfall in Conakry.

items.title: The Dominance of Facebook
items.text: Facebook is the primary internet for most Guineans. Brands often use Facebook Pages as their de facto customer service hubs and primary product catalogs.

items.title: Word-of-Mouth Reliability
items.text: In Guinea, physical community referrals (Radio Trottoir) are often more powerful than digital ads. Building local community trust through events is as vital as online presence.

items.title: Mobile-Video Consumption
items.text: TikTok usage has surged in 2024-2025. Short, lifestyle-focused videos in French with local music are currently the most effective way to reach the under-30 demographic.

items.title: The Power of Radio
items.text: While digital is growing, Radio remains 'King' in the interior regions. Campaigns must include a radio component (often in local languages like Peulh or Malinké) for national reach.

items.title: Regulatory Compliance (OGP)
items.text: All public advertising in Guinea must be approved by the 'Office Guinéen de Publicité' (OGP). There are specific taxes on billboards and TV ads that the agency must manage.

items.title: Corporate CSR Messaging
items.text: Guinean consumers respond very positively to brands that showcase CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) initiatives, particularly those related to education, water, or local sports.

faqs.question: Can we manage Guinean ads from Europe/USA?
faqs.answer: Technically yes for digital, but for local media buying and OOH, you need a local Guinean agency to navigate OGP regulations and ensure the best local rates.

faqs.question: Is English-language marketing effective?
faqs.answer: No. Except for very specific B2B niche mining services, all marketing should be in French. Using English conveys an 'outsider' image that may hinder trust.

faqs.question: What is the best time for TV/Radio ads?
faqs.answer: Primary prime time is during the 8:30 PM News (Journal télévisé) on RTG and morning commute hours (7:00 AM - 9:00 AM) for radio.
